scope: Three AWS agents and proposed shared operating patterns; no live execution or measured benefit.

devops.title: AWS DevOps Agent
devops.strapline: Incident investigation, service-status analysis and release-readiness workflows.
devops.audience: On-call engineers, SREs, platform engineers and service owners
devops.availability: Production operations: GA. Release management: preview; assess each feature and Region separately.
devops.decision: Start with one read-heavy investigation workflow. Add action paths only after the evidence and authorization boundaries have been tested.
summary: During an incident, the hard part is rarely opening another dashboard. It is connecting the affected service, the deployment that preceded the symptom, and the evidence that distinguishes a plausible explanation from the actual failure. DevOps Agent brings those sources into an investigation context; the engineer still decides whether the evidence justifies a mitigation.

This report follows an illustrative checkout failure after a retry-policy change. The useful result is not a fluent root-cause statement. It is a traceable investigation, a controlled next action, and a verification record. The same context can support daily health questions and prevention work. Release-readiness review and active release testing are a distinct preview path, not a capability that becomes generally available merely because production operations are GA.

use_case.name: Checkout errors after a retry-policy release
use_case.trigger: A supplied incident snapshot shows rising checkout 5xx errors after deployment DEMO-A.
use_case.scope: One team-owned service, explicit environment and UTC incident window, selected repositories and telemetry.
use_case.deliverable: Evidence-backed incident handoff with a mitigation candidate, owner, rollback assumptions and recovery checks.
use_case.not_done: The agent has written a plausible explanation, but the deployed revision and telemetry have not been compared.
use_case.done: The service owner has accepted or rejected the explanation, authorized any change separately, and recorded independent recovery evidence.

stages.title: Establish the operational boundary
paragraphs: Begin with the service and the incident window, not an unrestricted instruction to fix production. An Agent Space gathers account configuration, integrations and application context. Its topology helps the investigation understand relationships; underlying IAM and integration permissions determine what can actually be accessed.

Connect a known-good deployment reference and the telemetry needed to challenge the incident hypothesis. Missing logs are an evidence gap, not a reason to grant broad write permissions. Validate one expected read and one harmless out-of-scope denial before relying on the configuration.
stages.input: Service identity, environment, incident window, deployed revision, relevant telemetry and repository access.
stages.artifact: A scope record and a short inventory of available and missing evidence.
stages.gate: The service owner can explain the access boundary and identify who can stop the work.
stages.fallback: Keep the incident in the normal on-call process while missing evidence or permissions are repaired.

stages.title: Investigate, then challenge the explanation
paragraphs: An alert, ticket or on-demand question can start the operational workflow. Ask the agent to separate observations, hypotheses and missing data. For the checkout example, the deployment time, affected resources and request failures need to agree before the change becomes the leading explanation.

Use follow-up questions to test alternatives: an upstream timeout, a capacity limit, or an unrelated configuration change. A confident answer does not eliminate competing causes. The engineer compares material claims with the source systems and preserves the evidence links for the incident record.
stages.input: Incident signal and scoped operational context.
stages.artifact: A hypothesis ledger with supporting observations, contrary evidence and unresolved gaps.
stages.gate: At least one material claim is independently checked against its source.
stages.fallback: Record an inconclusive investigation rather than inventing a cause or waiting indefinitely.

stages.title: Separate a recommendation from an authorized action
paragraphs: A mitigation proposal should state the intended effect, blast radius, validation criteria and reversal plan. In the example, reducing retries may be a candidate, but a service owner must consider whether it hides errors or shifts load elsewhere. Recommendations are reviewable artifacts, not implicit permission to modify resources.

Directed actions have their own enablement, access and approval controls. Keep the action decision attached to the exact target and operation. An approval to investigate is not approval to deploy, and a broad instruction in chat is not a substitute for the configured authorization path.
stages.input: Reviewed hypothesis and a specific mitigation candidate.
stages.artifact: An action decision with owner, target, allowed effect, rollback and verification criteria.
stages.gate: The effect is authorized through the correct product and team controls.
stages.fallback: Execute through the established runbook or change process when the agent action path is not approved.

stages.title: Turn an incident into owned prevention work
paragraphs: After recovery, recurring incident patterns can inform observability, resilience, infrastructure and deployment improvements. Convert a useful recommendation into a bounded engineering item rather than leaving it as an unowned report. Preserve the original incident references so the proposed fix can be evaluated against the actual failure.

Daily health summaries are configured custom-agent workflows. Specify the question, tools, skills, schedule and audience explicitly. A scheduled prompt cannot see a database or monitoring system that has not been connected, and an automated summary still needs an owner who handles missing or stale data.
stages.input: Validated incident record, historical incidents and a named follow-up owner.
stages.artifact: A prioritized improvement item or configured recurring operational report.
stages.gate: The item has measurable acceptance criteria and the scheduled output has a recipient and stop owner.
stages.fallback: Use the existing backlog and manual report until the integrations provide adequate evidence.

stages.title: Review the next release without confusing the test paths
paragraphs: The follow-up retry-policy change can be reviewed for release risk. Readiness review evaluates a code change and its dependencies, policies and access implications; managed verification can add build or test evidence. These are release-preview features and should be piloted separately from the production investigation baseline.

Active release testing instead interacts with a running application. Browser or API requests can create, update or delete data and trigger business effects. Use a disposable staging target, test identities and disabled external side effects. Infrastructure write access being disabled does not make application testing read-only.
stages.input: Candidate revision, application context, and an authorized staging target where active testing is used.
stages.artifact: Release findings, reproduction details and explicit residual risks.
stages.gate: The release owner checks both feature availability and the actual effects allowed against the test target.
stages.fallback: Use prepared results or the ordinary test suite rather than testing a production endpoint to keep a demo moving.

stages.title: Hand off an operational work item and verify closure
paragraphs: The proposed team handoff turns an accepted investigation into an owned engineering work item. Include the incident window, affected service and revision, evidence references, remaining uncertainty and the required recovery check. Preparing a code or configuration change is a responsibility of the receiving engineering team; it is not an additional DevOps Agent capability claimed here.

Use the existing review and delivery process for any change. The service owner checks current telemetry after deployment, records whether the symptom recovered and reopens the investigation when the evidence does not support closure. A generated recommendation alone is not a completed incident.
stages.input: Evidence-linked issue with affected repository, constraints, test expectations and reviewer.
stages.artifact: Reviewed code or operational change plus a recovery or regression-test record.
stages.gate: A human reviewer accepts the result; deployment authority and access remain local to their own systems.
stages.fallback: Keep a failed or inconclusive change visible as unfinished work rather than closing the incident on generated text.

checks: One owned workload and UTC time window are recorded.
A deployed revision and material telemetry are available.
Out-of-scope access is denied at the actual integration layer.
Hypotheses and missing evidence are separated.
Any change has its own authorization, rollback and verifier.
Active release tests use an approved non-production target.

security.title: AWS Security Agent
security.strapline: Authorized application assessments, findings, remediation proposals and revalidation.
security.audience: Application-security engineers, software teams and security platform owners
security.availability: On-demand penetration testing: GA. Design review, threat modeling, code review and CI/CD integration are separate preview capabilities.
security.decision: Start with one explicitly authorized staging application. Assess the safety of real requests, then connect findings to reviewed repairs and revalidation.
summary: A security assessment is useful when the finding is understandable, the affected application is known, and the team can act on the evidence. An automatically generated severity label is not enough. The application owner needs a reproducible account of the issue, a repair decision and evidence that the repaired deployment no longer exhibits the tested behavior.

The running scenario is an authorized assessment of a staging application with synthetic data and test identities. It follows scope, testing, finding triage, proposed remediation and revalidation. Design and code analysis are presented as complementary preview paths, not as guarantees of complete coverage or interchangeable forms of penetration testing.

use_case.name: Assess and repair an owned staging application
use_case.trigger: A team wants evidence about an application change before deciding how to proceed with release.
use_case.scope: Verified targets, written authorization, test accounts, synthetic data, explicit exclusions and a stop owner.
use_case.deliverable: A triaged finding linked to the tested revision, a reviewed remediation proposal and revalidation evidence.
use_case.not_done: A generated fix exists, but it has not been reviewed, deployed to the test target or reassessed.
use_case.done: The authorized test, code review and revalidation records support an owner-approved disposition of the finding.

stages.title: Make authorization and target safety explicit
paragraphs: Define the application, exact target addresses, permitted test window, identities, exclusions and stop authority. Domain verification is a technical prerequisite; it is not permission from every system owner affected by a request. A staging label alone does not prove that payments, emails or other downstream effects are disabled.

Penetration testing sends real requests and can change application state. Use synthetic data and appropriately limited test identities, and understand the configured execution and spend controls. The demo should be possible without touching production or a third party outside the authorization.
stages.input: Written scope, verified target, test identities, approved network path and operational stop procedure.
stages.artifact: An assessment authorization and preflight record.
stages.gate: The owner has approved the targets and business effects, not merely a hostname.
stages.fallback: Stop preparation when authority or downstream effects are unclear; use a labeled schematic walkthrough instead.

stages.title: Give the assessment current application context
paragraphs: Source code, architecture documents and authentication details help the assessment understand the application. Keep the code revision aligned with the deployed test target. Old design documents or credentials for the wrong role can distort both coverage and interpretation.

Use the documented credential and private-connectivity paths rather than pasting secrets into example prompts or reports. Record what was reachable and authenticated. A test that did not reach a protected workflow cannot provide evidence that the workflow is safe.
stages.input: Current code and design context, revision identity, approved credentials and reachable test routes.
stages.artifact: A context and coverage record attached to the assessment.
stages.gate: The team knows which roles, routes and deployed revision were actually in scope.
stages.fallback: Report inaccessible areas as coverage gaps and resolve setup before drawing broader conclusions.

stages.title: Observe the run and triage the evidence
paragraphs: Monitor the authorized task and inspect findings as evidence about a particular application state. Prioritization should combine the reported impact, reproducibility, affected data or role, and the service owner's business context. Do not equate finding count with assessment quality.

Preserve the path from the observation to the affected revision and identity. A validated exploit path can be valuable, but a clean result is not proof that every vulnerability class or application route has been covered. Escalate uncertain findings for human review rather than turning uncertainty into a release assurance.
stages.input: Assessment execution details and finding evidence.
stages.artifact: A triaged finding with owner, affected scope, reproduction context and disposition.
stages.gate: The service owner understands the finding and the limits of the assessment.
stages.fallback: Pause or stop on unexpected effects and retain an incomplete-run record instead of treating it as a pass.

stages.title: Review a proposed repair as an engineering change
paragraphs: With the appropriate repository configuration, a finding can lead to a proposed code repair. That proposal needs normal review for correctness, compatibility and test coverage. A patch that blocks the observed path may still create a regression or leave a related path unresolved.

Track the finding and repair in the team's existing issue system. A Jira handoff is useful only when the audience is appropriate and the ticket links the evidence, affected revision and acceptance test. Do not publish sensitive assessment details to a broader channel simply because an integration is connected.
stages.input: Accepted finding, permitted repository access and a repair owner.
stages.artifact: A reviewed PR/MR or repair plan linked to the original finding.
stages.gate: The proposed change passes independent review and normal delivery controls.
stages.fallback: Assign a manual repair when repository support, authorization or generated output is inadequate.

stages.title: Deploy to the authorized target and revalidate
paragraphs: A code fix is not the same as a repaired deployed application. Record the revision deployed to the authorized test target before requesting revalidation. Compare the result with the original evidence and confirm that the targeted behavior is no longer reproducible under the intended conditions.

Export a point-in-time report that preserves the scope, results and unresolved limitations. Closing the issue is an owner decision supported by assessment evidence, code review and revalidation. None of those artifacts alone is a certificate that the application is secure.
stages.input: Reviewed repair deployed to the approved target and linked to the original finding.
stages.artifact: Revalidation outcome and point-in-time evidence report.
stages.gate: The closure decision identifies the tested revision and remaining risks.
stages.fallback: Keep the finding open or explicitly risk-accepted if revalidation is inconclusive or fails.

stages.title: Add earlier feedback without overstating availability
paragraphs: Design reviews, organizational security requirements and threat models can make assumptions and trust boundaries inspectable before testing a running application. Code review can analyze full repositories or configured change triggers, with provider-specific remediation paths. These are distinct from the GA on-demand penetration-testing baseline.

Treat S3 differential-scan and CI/CD integrations as separate preview adoption decisions. A promotion gate needs explicit thresholds, timeout behavior and a policy for missing or inconclusive evidence. The team owns that release policy; an unavailable or unfinished scan should not silently become a green gate.
stages.input: Approved preview use, provider-specific integration and an explicit review or promotion policy.
stages.artifact: Design, threat-model or code findings and an auditable gate decision where configured.
stages.gate: Availability, source-provider support and failure behavior are checked for the exact workflow.
stages.fallback: Retain the existing review and security checks until the preview path is accepted for the intended use.

checks: Written authorization covers every target and relevant downstream effect.
The test uses synthetic data and limited test identities.
Source context and deployed revision agree.
Execution, budget and stop ownership are configured.
Findings and generated repairs receive independent review.
Revalidation and closure identify the tested repaired revision.

finops.title: AWS FinOps Agent
finops.strapline: Cost analysis, anomaly investigation, reporting and engineering follow-up.
finops.audience: FinOps practitioners, platform engineers and service owners
finops.availability: The entire service is preview. Review the documented US storage and inference boundary before supplying organizational data.
finops.decision: Start with one cost question whose total can be independently reproduced. Keep infrastructure changes and financial commitments outside the analysis authority.
summary: The first question after a cost increase is not which resource to delete. It is whether the compared figures use the same period, account scope, currency and cost basis. Only then can the team decide whether the movement reflects usage, pricing, allocation, a change in workload behavior or incomplete data.

This report follows a synthetic storage-cost increase from reconciliation to a service-owned action. FinOps Agent can support inquiry, anomaly investigation, recommendation triage and reporting through permitted cost services. The analysis does not authorize a capacity change or purchase. Potential savings remain estimates until an implemented change is measured on a comparable basis.

use_case.name: Explain a synthetic storage-cost increase
use_case.trigger: A teaching dataset compares two complete 14-day periods and shows approximately 41% higher cost.
use_case.scope: Explicit accounts, Regions, currency, date boundaries, tags and cost metric; synthetic figures are not an AWS account result.
use_case.deliverable: A reconciled explanation, confidence and gaps, an engineering owner and a controlled follow-up.
use_case.not_done: An attractive savings estimate is quoted without matching totals or checking operational constraints.
use_case.done: The source total is reproducible, the driver is supported by evidence, and an owner accepts the next action and measurement plan.

stages.title: Define the comparison before asking for an explanation
paragraphs: Write down the cost metric, currency, account group, Region filters and complete date windows. Clarify whether the comparison includes credits, refunds, amortization or allocation rules. Organizational context can identify owners and services, but it does not repair inconsistent billing filters.

Approve preview use and the documented processing boundary before uploading internal context. IAM and permitted cost services determine accessible data. Start with an account group whose owner can validate a material total rather than granting broad access to make every possible question answerable.
stages.input: Comparison contract, approved data scope and current ownership context.
stages.artifact: A reproducible cost-query definition with explicit exclusions.
stages.gate: The same query can be expressed in the underlying source service.
stages.fallback: Resolve metric or date mismatches before discussing causes or savings.

stages.title: Reconcile the total and identify material contributors
paragraphs: Ask the agent to group the cost by useful dimensions and show the arithmetic behind the movement. Reproduce at least one material total in the source system using the same filters. A convincing explanation based on a different cost basis is not acceptable evidence.

Forecasts and commitment coverage can provide additional context, but they answer different questions from historical reconciliation. Separate observed spend from forecast values and contractual estimates. The synthetic demo illustrates this distinction; it is not evidence of a real account anomaly.
stages.input: Matching cost queries for both comparison periods.
stages.artifact: A reconciled delta and a ranked set of contributing services or usage dimensions.
stages.gate: Totals, scope and arithmetic agree with an independent source check.
stages.fallback: Label unresolved discrepancies and withhold a causal conclusion until the totals are understood.

stages.title: Investigate drivers without mistaking correlation for cause
paragraphs: An anomaly investigation can combine cost evidence with permitted operational context, including relevant change records. Ask which observations support a likely driver, which alternatives remain plausible, and which evidence is missing. A deployment occurring near the increase is a lead, not proof of causation.

Event-triggered investigation is a configured workflow. Confirm the anomaly event source, permissions and output destination, and decide how duplicate or incomplete events are handled. The team still needs an owner who reviews the result and can stop a noisy automation.
stages.input: Reconciled movement, anomaly details and permitted change context.
stages.artifact: A driver analysis that separates observations, hypotheses and gaps.
stages.gate: The proposed explanation accounts for a material part of the observed change.
stages.fallback: Route an unresolved question to the workload owner instead of inventing a definitive cause.

stages.title: Evaluate recommendations against operational constraints
paragraphs: Existing optimization recommendations can help prioritize investigation, but their projected savings are not an instruction to implement. Review utilization, resilience, performance and recovery requirements with the service owner. Avoid adding overlapping estimates as though every action can deliver its full saving independently.

For a storage recommendation, clarify whether the action changes retention, retrieval latency, durability assumptions or recovery procedures. The authorized change belongs in normal infrastructure and financial processes. The agent's useful output is a justified candidate with constraints and evidence.
stages.input: Recommendation source, utilization evidence, service constraints and estimated benefit.
stages.artifact: A prioritized candidate with operational risks, owner and acceptance criteria.
stages.gate: The service owner accepts the trade-offs and the change is approved separately.
stages.fallback: Reject or defer recommendations that conflict with the service's reliability or data obligations.

stages.title: Publish the result to the right audience
paragraphs: Turn the analysis into a report or tracked task with the comparison basis, important figures, uncertainty and next owner. Recurring reporting is useful when its schedule and audience are explicit. Context files and remembered preferences should be reviewed when ownership or reporting rules change.

Jira and Slack are external publication effects, not merely read-only analysis. Interactive Jira confirmation, automated-task behavior and Slack posting controls differ. Review the documented path and the destination audience before scheduling a task or sharing commercially sensitive cost information.
stages.input: Reviewed analysis, approved destination and named action owner.
stages.artifact: A report or ticket with evidence links and a concrete next step.
stages.gate: Audience, automatic-posting behavior and approval expectations match the chosen integration.
stages.fallback: Keep the result in a local report until the publication path and audience are approved.

stages.title: Measure an implemented change on a comparable basis
paragraphs: After an independently authorized engineering change, compare the relevant cost and service indicators using a consistent measurement basis. Separate savings caused by the change from lower traffic, different prices or changed allocation. A smaller invoice alone does not establish that the recommendation delivered the estimated benefit.

Close the task only when the owner has reviewed both cost and operational outcomes. Capture rejected recommendations and analysis effort as well as accepted work. That gives the pilot a more meaningful scorecard than the number of reports produced or the sum of potential savings shown.
stages.input: Implemented change record, comparable observation windows and service-health evidence.
stages.artifact: A measured outcome with attribution limits and an owner-approved disposition.
stages.gate: Benefit and reliability implications are checked independently of the original recommendation.
stages.fallback: Leave benefit unclaimed when the comparison cannot isolate the effect or required data is incomplete.

checks: Preview use and data-location boundaries are approved.
Periods, currency, filters and cost basis are explicit.
A material total reconciles to the source service.
Observed movement is separated from causal hypotheses.
Publication destinations and automation behavior are reviewed.
Changes and purchases require separate approval; savings are not pre-claimed.

architecture.title: Common architectural patterns
architecture.strapline: Common work contracts, evidence, authorization and verification patterns across three products.
architecture.audience: Platform architects, engineering leads, security governance and service owners
architecture.availability: Team-level synthesis of documented mechanisms. Not an AWS shared runtime, unified permission model or implemented multi-agent orchestrator.
architecture.decision: Standardize scope, evidence, ownership and acceptance first. Automate a handoff only after its specialist boundaries work reliably without automation.
summary: The three agents do different jobs and expose different execution surfaces. A useful common architecture does not hide those differences. It defines what a task means, where evidence comes from, which effects are permitted, who owns the decision and how the result is verified.

The running tabletop begins with a checkout incident and ends with a reviewed implementation and independent verification. Security and cost assessments are conditional branches, not mandatory calls to every agent. The connecting artifact is an existing incident, issue or change record. Credentials and approvals are deliberately not passed along with it.

use_case.name: An incident-to-change handoff across specialist boundaries
use_case.trigger: An operator has evidence of a checkout failure and a bounded implementation task.
use_case.scope: One workload, named owners, selected specialist tasks and explicit allowed effects.
use_case.deliverable: A chain of evidence-linked work items whose results and authorization decisions can be reconstructed.
use_case.not_done: Several agents have generated compatible-looking summaries, but there is no independent verification or accountable owner.
use_case.done: Each specialist's result is accepted against its contract, every effect is locally authorized, and the final outcome is independently checked.

stages.title: Choose a specialist and write the work contract
paragraphs: Start with the evidence and outcome required. DevOps Agent supports operational investigations, Security Agent supports authorized application assessments, and FinOps Agent supports cost analysis. Select only the specialist needed for the task. Code implementation, merge and deployment remain assigned engineering responsibilities rather than an additional agent role in this collection.

The proposed common contract records the workload, owner, task, allowed effects, exclusions, completion checks and stop responsibility. A product workspace or prompt is not proof that access is enforced. Test the actual IAM, repository and integration boundaries used by the chosen specialist.
stages.input: An owned engineering problem and the smallest useful specialist task.
stages.artifact: A bounded work contract with exact accounts, repositories or targets.
stages.gate: The owner can identify the result needed and the effects that are not permitted.
stages.fallback: Use a manual specialist workflow until scope and ownership are unambiguous.

stages.title: Assemble evidence with provenance
paragraphs: Collect the source references needed to evaluate the task: incident window, deployed revision, repository branch, assessment target or cost-query basis. Preserve timestamps, scope and known gaps so the next reviewer can reproduce a material observation rather than trusting a summary.

Steering, skills, instructions and memory can guide work, but they are not authorization grants or substitutes for current evidence. Treat external documents, tool outputs and repository content as potentially untrusted input. Separate what the agent is told from what its identity is allowed to do.
stages.input: Relevant source records and clearly labeled instructions or organizational context.
stages.artifact: An evidence packet with provenance, freshness and unresolved questions.
stages.gate: A material claim can be traced to an accessible source in the correct scope.
stages.fallback: Mark the result inconclusive when the source record is absent, stale or contradictory.

stages.title: Classify the effect before selecting the control
paragraphs: Reading telemetry, editing a branch, sending a request to an application and posting a report are different effects. Their approval requirements should not be flattened into a single idea of human oversight. In particular, an isolated worker can still act against a live target, and an analytical task can still publish sensitive information externally.

Evaluate availability, entitlement, Region, data handling and target safety for the exact feature. The GA label of one product path does not apply to its preview features. Keep the action-control matrix explicit enough that operators can tell what requires approval and what may run automatically once configured.
stages.input: Intended effect, target, product surface and data-location requirements.
stages.artifact: An effect-specific authorization and isolation decision.
stages.gate: Worker controls, target controls and output audience are all understood.
stages.fallback: Reduce to a read-only or draft-only path when the required authority is not available.

stages.title: Run a bounded job with a stop owner
paragraphs: A documented API, integration or remote protocol can be an adapter between systems; it does not establish a universal agent-to-agent transaction. Choose only the interfaces needed for the task and retain each product's access model. Manual handoff is a valid first implementation.

Bound the job's time, spend, retries and concurrency where the product provides controls, and add team procedures where it does not. A recurring schedule needs a recipient, duplicate-work policy and stop owner. Record partial and failed outcomes rather than treating lack of a response as success.
stages.input: Authorized task, explicit adapter and operational limits.
stages.artifact: A run record with status, owner, effect log and stop or retry decision.
stages.gate: Operators can interrupt work and identify incomplete results.
stages.fallback: Use a prepared, labeled example for presentations and the established engineering process for real work.

stages.title: Transfer a reviewable artifact—not inherited privileges
paragraphs: For an incident-to-fix handoff, the next specialist receives the affected repository, observed failure, evidence references and regression-test expectations. It does not receive production credentials or a blanket instruction to implement every mitigation. A security finding or cost recommendation follows the same artifact principle.

Keep work-item IDs, source revisions and reviewer decisions stable across systems of record. The receiving specialist establishes its own authorized access and acceptance criteria. That preserves accountability even when the handoff is automated later.
stages.input: Accepted specialist output with scope, evidence and unresolved limitations.
stages.artifact: A linked implementation, assessment or optimization task with a new accountable owner.
stages.gate: The recipient can evaluate the result without inheriting the sender's approval authority.
stages.fallback: Reject an incomplete handoff and request missing evidence instead of filling gaps with assumptions.

stages.title: Verify independently before widening the system
paragraphs: Verification must be independent of the claim being accepted. Compare an incident conclusion with telemetry, a code change with meaningful tests and review, a repaired finding with revalidation, and a cost recommendation with a consistent post-change measurement. Agent agreement alone is not independent verification.

Pilot one workflow before building a broad orchestrator. Measure acceptance, rework, boundary failures, time spent reviewing and the quality of retained evidence. Expand only where the operating process is understood and the chosen interfaces and feature availability support it.
stages.input: Specialist output and an independent acceptance method.
stages.artifact: An owner-approved outcome and evidence-based expansion decision.
stages.gate: The final decision can be reconstructed from sources, controls and verification records.
stages.fallback: Keep the workflow manual or narrow its scope when evidence or control reliability is inadequate.

checks: Every task has a workload owner, scope and completion check.
Evidence retains timestamps, revision and provenance.
Instructions and memory are not treated as access grants.
Approval is specific to the effect, target and interface.
Jobs have limits, stop ownership and an incomplete-result path.
Handoffs transfer artifacts rather than credentials or inherited approval.
An independent check supports each accepted result.
Feature availability and data location are reviewed separately.
